extracted.intended_audience: architects, art historians, students of architecture, and general readers interested in architectural aesthetics and criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for judging Venetian (and comparative Gothic vs Renaissance) architecture and related arts — focusing on form, ornament, material honesty, execution, and the moral/aesthetic virtues that constitute beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance (broad aesthetic virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperance, in the broadest sense, is the safeguard of highest beauty in all visible work; it governs intense energy and prevents its acting otherwise than it ought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin explains temperance as not dulling enjoyment but regulating quantity so enjoyment is greatest. It is the virtue that controls color, curvature, and ornament so that the work attains maximum beauty without excess. Anti-pattern: indulgent, unregulated use of any element that jades the eye or feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance in color
rubrics_metrics.description: Color must be governed so as to bring the utmost possible enjoyment out of all hues rather than used in large, unsubdued masses that jades the eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice: build work from sober browns and dull greys, extract life from them, then permit momentary crimson and azure as a crown of the work. Anti-pattern: using overly vivid color in great quantity so it becomes greyed and lifeless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance in curvature / line
rubrics_metrics.description: Curvature should be long before it is perceived and restrained; the great designer avoids violent curves and uses subdued curvatures opposed by firmer lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good design dwells on subdued curvatures and reserves abrupt curves for moments of energy. Anti-pattern: continual violent and unrestrained curvatures that roll 'hither and thither' indicating exhausted invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of luxuriance / over-lusciousness of ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Luxuriance of ornament is not mere quantity but a character of extravagance—violence and coarseness in curvature, depth of shadow, and luscious arrangement—which shows the ornament is addressed to jaded faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify excessive ornament by its aim to excite a satiated eye; contrast with chaste, restrained ornament where even dense sculpture remains noble. Anti-pattern: ornament that is wanton, morbidly excited, or merely sensual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of ornament to building spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornament and minor features must be consistent with the general spirit and massing of the building (e.g., finial is proper to gabled architecture but contradictory to Venetian horizontal building).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether an added detail (finial, crocket, enriched moulding) coheres with the building's structural and typological spirit. Anti-pattern: adopting motifs inconsistent with overall form, producing contradiction and signs of decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finials and crockets as signs of decline when misapplied
rubrics_metrics.description: The adoption and extravagant development of finials and crockets in Venice—where building is horizontal—indicate morbid excitement and architectural decline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: enormous finials half as high as arches, human figures emerging from leaf-cups; when these appear on non-gabled Venetian work they mark corruption. Use as diagnostic features of decay rather than neutral ornaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enrichment/complication of jamb mouldings (contextual diagnosis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive enrichment and complication of jamb mouldings, when inconsistent with ancient Venetian single square jamb and archivolt, are signs of decline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare successive examples (as Ruskin does in plates) to judge whether enrichment is a healthy development or a degenerative corruption. Anti-pattern: piling up mouldings that contradict established structural idiom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between breadth and subdivision
rubrics_metrics.description: Both breadth and subdivision can be noble depending on the healthy mind that conceived them; excessive subdivision or unwholesome breadth may indicate failure of taste or decay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breadth is appropriate to broad wall surfaces; subdivision suits delicate contexts. Anti-patterns: pointless subdivision that cuts broad noble forms to pieces (sign of inability to relish simplicity) or heavy broad forms that are blunt and dead from lack of refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalism/animation versus formalized conventionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturalistic, living forms (e.g., leaves as if fresh gathered) indicate health in style; severe conventionalized forms (Byzantine stiffness) are colder; both may be temperate, but the Gothic's temperance was nobler due to animation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge foliage, capitals, tracery by degree of living naturalism and animation; healthy development shows progressive animation from severity to living line. Anti-pattern: formalized, stagnant conventionality lacking life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty of materials and use of marbles
rubrics_metrics.description: Using materials to deceive (plaster made to look like marble, or marble carved to look like silk) is a mean and vulgar abuse; true art values color and merit above mere costly imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer honest expression of materials; suspicious where imitation or 'juggling' for its own sake replaces aesthetic judgment. Anti-pattern: delight in falsehood or in marble manipulated solely to exhibit costliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate relation of ornament to structural truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornament should arise from and be consistent with structural forms (clustered shafts, pointed arches) rather than be superimposed classical decoration onto incompatible Gothic structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether ornament respects the building's structural logic; when Renaissance classical elements sweep away Gothic structural systems (pointed arch, clustered shaft), form becomes cold and meagre in outline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism of universal demand for technical perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: An imperative requirement for consummate execution in everything (the Renaissance demand for universal perfection) leads to loss of tenderness, originality, and the soul of work when copied by lesser hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate works by true masters (where perfection serves invention) from commonplace copyists who attain finish at the cost of invention. Anti-pattern: valuing finish/technique over feeling/original thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between execution/knowledge and originality/feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy and dexterity are valuable, but should not supplant originality and feeling; a work can be consummately finished yet utterly inanimate if created by the minor workman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both technical finish and presence of invention; be wary of technically perfect yet soulless architecture ('a base and helpless copy of more accomplished models').

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility of classical forms with architectural purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical/Roman forms (round arch, cross-beam, pediment) are not always appropriate replacements for Gothic elements; certain Roman elements (cupola, internal wagon vault) are exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge changes in form by how they serve structural and artistic ends. Anti-pattern: wholesale substitution of classical outlines for Gothic structure resulting in cold, meagre silhouette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ornament as moral/aesthetic indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornamental character corresponds to moral character: overcharged ornament can correspond to intemperance; restraint corresponds to virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read ornament as symptomatic of cultural and moral states (e.g., decadence, jaded energy). Anti-pattern: treating ornament purely as surface without moral/aesthetic diagnosis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of types of Renaissance influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruskin distinguishes Early Renaissance (corruptions introduced into Gothic), Central/Roman Renaissance (perfectly formed classical style), and Grotesque Renaissance (excessive, degenerate forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a building, identify which Renaissance strand it exemplifies to understand whether changes are corrective, corrupting, or grotesque. Use typology to diagnose quality and historical cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic features of architectural decline
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific features that indicate decline include morbid finials and crockets, redundant curvature, luxurious subdivision, extravagant traceries, and enriched jambs inconsistent with type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these features as concrete signs when judging whether later work represents healthy development or decadence; compare with earlier noble examples (e.g., Ducal Palace) to see divergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for appropriate scale and massing
rubrics_metrics.description: Mouldings, foliage, and capitals must harmonize with the scale and mass of the wall or building surface (e.g., broad foliage to match mighty wall surfaces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether decorative scale is in dialogue with structural mass; anti-pattern: small, intricate foliage on large, heroic surfaces, or vice versa, producing disharmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic honesty in painting and conservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Paintings should be judged by original conception, temperance in treatment, truthful attention to nature, and care against destructive repainting or academy re-handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of works ruined by repainting or academic retouch that obscure the master's hand; value temperate, well-lit, truthfully observed works (Ruskin praises certain Tintoret examples for temperance and truthful nature).
